cards.front: What is prompt engineering (in this book)?
cards.back: Crafting an instruction that gets a foundation model to produce the desired output without changing model weights.
The model adapts behavior from examples placed in the prompt—no weight updates. Also called few-shot when examples are included.
Zero-shot: no examples in the prompt. Few-shot: one or more demonstration examples (shots) before the task.
System: developer-defined rules, persona, format. User: end-user query plus retrieved/uploaded context. APIs concatenate via a model-specific chat template.

cards.front: Needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) — where do models often recall best?
cards.back: At the start and end of long context; performance is often weaker in the middle (Liu et al., 2023).
Step-by-step reasoning before the final answer—e.g. “think step by step”—to improve math and reasoning tasks at higher latency/cost.
Jailbreaking: bypass safety policies. Prompt injection: malicious instructions in user or tool content to hijack behavior. Huyen uses “jailbreaking” broadly for both.
System > developer > user > model output > tool output—reduces some injection success when trained into the model.

choices: Examples in the prompt without weight updates
questions.explanation: ICL (Brown et al., 2020) adapts at inference time via the prompt, not gradient updates.

questions.prompt: Decomposing a complex task into smaller prompts mainly helps with:
questions.explanation: Chains trade more queries for easier debugging and routing (e.g. intent → specialized prompts).
Syntax ≠ semantics—you still need evaluation and validation.

questions.prompt: For long-context RAG, critical facts are often placed:
choices: Only in the system prompt footer
questions.explanation: NIAH shows U-shaped recall; structure prompts and retrieval accordingly.

questions.prompt: Indirect prompt injection hides instructions in:
questions.explanation: Especially risky for agents and RAG where untrusted text becomes prompt content.

choices: Model training, prompt design, and system guardrails
questions.explanation: Huyen advocates layers: instruction hierarchy, isolation, human approval, I/O filters—not one silver bullet.
